questions.description: Questions to ask the user (1-4 questions)

question.description: The complete question to ask the user. Should be clear, specific, and end with a question mark. Example: "Which library should we use for date formatting?" If multiSelect is true, phrase it accordingly, e.g. "Which features do you want to enable?"

header.description: Very short label displayed as a chip/tag (max 12 chars). Examples: "Auth method", "Library", "Approach".

options.description: The available choices for this question. Must have 2-4 options. Each option should be a distinct, mutually exclusive choice (unless multiSelect is enabled). There should be no 'Other' option, that will be provided automatically.

label.description: The display text for this option that the user will see and select. Should be concise (1-5 words) and clearly describe the choice.

description.description: Explanation of what this option means or what will happen if chosen. Useful for providing context about trade-offs or implications.

preview.description: Optional preview content rendered when this option is focused. Use for mockups, code snippets, or visual comparisons that help users compare options. See the tool description for the expected content format.

multiSelect.description: Set to true to allow the user to select multiple options instead of just one. Use when choices are not mutually exclusive.

answers.description: User answers collected by the permission component

annotations.description: Optional per-question annotations from the user (e.g., notes on preview selections). Keyed by question text.

preview.description: The preview content of the selected option, if the question used previews.

notes.description: Free-text notes the user added to their selection.

metadata.description: Optional metadata for tracking and analytics purposes. Not displayed to user.

source.description: Optional identifier for the source of this question (e.g., "remember" for /remember command). Used for analytics tracking.

tools.name: Bash
tools.description:
Executes a bash command and returns its output.

This tool runs Git Bash (POSIX sh), not cmd.exe or PowerShell. Use Unix shell syntax: `/dev/null` not `NUL`, forward slashes, `$VAR` not `%VAR%` or `$env:VAR`. Do not use PowerShell here-strings (`@'…'@`) or backtick continuation here — for multi-line strings use a heredoc.

- `cd` carries to the next call only in the main session, if the command succeeds and ends inside the working directories. Outside them the shell returns to the start folder; otherwise it stays where it was. Prefer absolute paths — `cd` in a compound command can trigger a permission prompt. Shell state (env vars, functions) does not persist; the shell is initialized from the user's profile.
- Command output is displayed to you, not reliably to the user.
- `timeout` is in milliseconds: default 120000, max 600000 for a foreground command.
- `run_in_background` runs the command detached: it keeps running across turns and re-invokes you when it exits. No `&` needed. You will be notified when it exits — do not poll its output file while waiting. Foreground `sleep` is blocked; use Monitor with an until-loop to wait on a condition.

# Git
- Interactive flags (`-i`, e.g. `git rebase -i`, `git add -i`) are not supported in this environment.
- Use the `gh` CLI for GitHub operations (PRs, issues, API).
- GitHub notifies the owner of any `@name` written in a PR, issue, or comment. Write a bare `@name` only for a real login you mean to notify. Put roles, placeholders, and code (`@human`, `@reviewer`, `@types/node`) in backticks or drop the `@`, even when copied from project files.
- Commit or push only when the user asks. If on the default branch, branch first.
- Do not commit files that likely contain secrets (.env, credentials.json, .claude/settings.local.json, etc). Warn the user if they specifically request to commit those files.
- End git commit messages and PR bodies with the attribution lines given in the conversation's system-reminder, when one is present.

timeout.description: Optional timeout in milliseconds (max 600000 for a foreground command)

description.description:
Clear, concise description of what this command does in active voice. Never use words like "complex" or "risk" in the description - just describe what it does.

Say what the command does in plain words: do not echo the command's text, its flags, or file paths - the user reads this description, often without seeing the command.

For simple commands (git, npm, standard CLI tools), keep it brief (5-10 words):
- ls → "List files in current directory"
- git status → "Show working tree status"
- npm install → "Install package dependencies"

For commands that are harder to parse at a glance (piped commands, obscure flags, etc.), add enough context to clarify what it does:
- find . -name "*.tmp" -exec rm {} \; → "Find and delete all .tmp files recursively"
- git reset --hard origin/main → "Discard all local changes and match remote main"
- curl -s url | jq '.data[]' → "Fetch JSON from URL and extract data array elements"

run_in_background.description: Set to true to run this command in the background.

dangerouslyDisableSandbox.description: Set this to true to dangerously override sandbox mode and run commands without sandboxing.

tools.name: Edit
tools.description:
Performs exact string replacement in a file.

- You must Read the file in this conversation before editing, or the call will fail.
- `old_string` must match the file exactly, including indentation, and be unique — the edit fails otherwise. Strip the Read line prefix (line number + tab) before matching.
- `replace_all: true` replaces every occurrence instead.

pattern.description: The glob pattern to match files against

path.description: The directory to search in. If not specified, the current working directory will be used. IMPORTANT: Omit this field to use the default directory. DO NOT enter "undefined" or "null" - simply omit it for the default behavior. Must be a valid directory path if provided.

tools.name: Grep
tools.description:
Content search built on ripgrep. Prefer this over `grep`/`rg` via Bash — results integrate with the permission UI and file links.

- Full regex syntax (e.g. "log.*Error", "function\s+\w+"). Ripgrep, not grep — escape literal braces (`interface\{\}`).
- Filter with `glob` (e.g. "**/*.tsx") or `type` (e.g. "js", "py", "rust").
- `output_mode`: "content" (matching lines), "files_with_matches" (paths only, default), or "count".
- `multiline: true` for patterns that span lines.

pattern.description: The regular expression pattern to search for in file contents

path.description: File or directory to search in (rg PATH). Defaults to current working directory.

glob.description: Glob pattern to filter files (e.g. "*.js", "*.{ts,tsx}") - maps to rg --glob

output_mode.description: Output mode: "content" shows matching lines (supports -A/-B/-C context, -n line numbers, head_limit), "files_with_matches" shows file paths (supports head_limit), "count" shows match counts (supports head_limit). Defaults to "files_with_matches".

-B.description: Number of lines to show before each match (rg -B). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise.

-A.description: Number of lines to show after each match (rg -A). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise.

context.description: Number of lines to show before and after each match (rg -C). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise.

-n.description: Show line numbers in output (rg -n). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise. Defaults to true.

-o.description: Print only the matched (non-empty) parts of each matching line, one match per output line (rg -o / --only-matching). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise. Defaults to false.

type.description: File type to search (rg --type). Common types: js, py, rust, go, java, etc. More efficient than include for standard file types.

head_limit.description: Limit output to first N lines/entries, equivalent to "| head -N". Works across all output modes: content (limits output lines), files_with_matches (limits file paths), count (limits count entries). Defaults to 250 when unspecified. Pass 0 for unlimited (use sparingly — large result sets waste context).

offset.description: Skip first N lines/entries before applying head_limit, equivalent to "| tail -n +N | head -N". Works across all output modes. Defaults to 0.

multiline.description: Enable multiline mode where . matches newlines and patterns can span lines (rg -U --multiline-dotall). Default: false.

tools.name: PowerShell
tools.description:
Executes a given PowerShell command with optional timeout. Working directory persists between commands; shell state (variables, functions) does not.

IMPORTANT: This tool is for terminal operations via PowerShell: git, npm, docker, and PS cmdlets. DO NOT use it for file operations (reading, writing, editing, searching, finding files) - use the specialized tools for this instead.

PowerShell edition: Windows PowerShell 5.1 (powershell.exe)
   - Pipeline chain operators `&&` and `||` are NOT available — they cause a parser error. To run B only if A succeeds: `A; if ($?) { B }`. To chain unconditionally: `A; B`.
   - Ternary (`?:`), null-coalescing (`??`), and null-conditional (`?.`) operators are NOT available. Use `if/else` and explicit `$null -eq` checks instead.
   - Avoid `2>&1` on native executables. In 5.1, redirecting a native command's stderr inside PowerShell wraps each line in an ErrorRecord (NativeCommandError) and sets `$?` to `$false` even when the exe returned exit code 0. stderr is already captured for you — don't redirect it.
   - `>`, `>>`, and `Out-File` usually default to UTF-8 (with BOM) in this environment, but `Set-Content`/`Add-Content` still default to the system ANSI codepage — when writing a file other tools will read, pass `-Encoding utf8` explicitly to `Out-File`/`Set-Content`.
   - `ConvertFrom-Json` returns a PSCustomObject, not a hashtable. `-AsHashtable` is not available.

Before executing the command, please follow these steps:

1. Directory Verification:
   - If the command will create new directories or files, first use `Get-ChildItem` (or `ls`) to verify the parent directory exists and is the correct location

2. Command Execution:
   - Always quote file paths that contain spaces with double quotes
   - Capture the output of the command.

PowerShell Syntax Notes:
   - Variables use $ prefix: $myVar = "value"
   - Escape character is backtick (`), not backslash
   - Use Verb-Noun cmdlet naming: Get-ChildItem, Set-Location, New-Item, Remove-Item
   - Common aliases: ls (Get-ChildItem), cd (Set-Location), cat (Get-Content), rm (Remove-Item)
   - Give helper functions a new Verb-Noun name such as Read-Doc, also in script files. A built-in alias (rd, rm, del, ri, sc, mv and others) runs instead of a function with the same name, with no warning.
   - Pipe operator | works similarly to bash but passes objects, not text
   - Use Select-Object, Where-Object, ForEach-Object for filtering and transformation
   - String interpolation: "Hello $name" or "Hello $($obj.Property)"
   - Registry access uses PSDrive prefixes: `HKLM:\SOFTWARE\...`, `HKCU:\...` — NOT raw `HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\...`
   - Environment variables: read with `$env:NAME`, set with `$env:NAME = "value"` (NOT `Set-Variable` or bash `export`)
   - Call native exe with spaces in path via call operator: `& "C:\Program Files\App\app.exe" arg1 arg2`

Unix commands that DO NOT exist in PowerShell — use the equivalent instead:
   - head / tail → `Get-Content file -TotalCount N` / `-Tail N`; piped: `| Select-Object -First N` / `-Last N`
   - which → `(Get-Command name).Source`
   - touch → `if (-not (Test-Path path)) { New-Item -ItemType File path }` (NEVER use `New-Item -Force` on a file — it truncates existing content)
   - wc -l → `(Get-Content file | Measure-Object -Line).Lines`
   - mkdir -p → `New-Item -ItemType Directory -Force path` (`-p` is not a PowerShell flag)
   - rm -rf → `Remove-Item -Recurse -Force path`
   - ln -s → `New-Item -ItemType SymbolicLink -Path link -Target target`
   - chmod / chown → not applicable on Windows; use `icacls` only if ACL changes are required
   - 2>/dev/null → `2>$null` (but stderr is captured for you — usually unnecessary)
   - VAR=x cmd → `$env:VAR = 'x'; cmd` (PowerShell has no inline env-var prefix)
   - Bash control flow (`if [ -f x ]`, `for x in *`, backtick ``cmd`` substitution) is a parser error — use `if (Test-Path x)`, `foreach ($x in ...)`, `$(cmd)`

Exit-code note: `-ErrorAction SilentlyContinue` suppresses error OUTPUT but the cmdlet failure still causes this tool to report exit 1. To make a cmdlet failure truly non-fatal, promote it to terminating and swallow it: `try { Cmdlet ... -ErrorAction Stop } catch {}` (without `-ErrorAction Stop`, non-terminating errors skip the `catch` and still exit 1).

   - String interpolation: "Hello $name" or "Hello $($obj.Property)"

tools.name: Read
tools.description:
Reads a file from the local filesystem.

- `file_path` must be an absolute path.
- Reads up to 2000 lines by default.
- When you already know which part of the file you need, only read that part. This can be important for larger files.
- Results are returned using cat -n format, with line numbers starting at 1
- Reads images (PNG, JPG, …) and presents them visually. Reads PDFs via the `pages` parameter (e.g. "1-5", max 20 pages/request; required for PDFs over 10 pages). Reads Jupyter notebooks (.ipynb) as cells with outputs.
- Reading a directory, a missing file, or an empty file returns an error or system reminder rather than content.
- Do NOT re-read a file you just edited to verify — Edit/Write would have errored if the change failed, and the harness tracks file state for you.

tools.name: ScheduleWakeup
tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use a 1-hour Anthropic prompt-cache TTL, so effectively every allowed delay (the runtime clamps to [60, 3600]) wakes up with your conversation context still cached. There is no cache cliff inside that range to pace around, and scheduling extra wakeups just to keep the cache warm is pure waste — never do that. (If the session enters usage overage, later requests drop to the 5-minute TTL; don't try to track or preempt that — the guidance here stays the same.)

Match the delay to what you're actually waiting for:

- **Actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about** (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue): pick the delay from how fast that state actually changes. A CI run that takes ~8 minutes deserves one ~480s check, not eight 60s ones.
- **The long fallback heartbeat** (something else — a Monitor, a task notification — is the primary wake signal): 1200s+, so quiet wakeups stay rare.
- **Idle ticks with no specific signal to watch**: default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop still checks back regularly, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Don't think in cache windows — think about what you're actually waiting for.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

tools.name: SendFeedback
tools.description:
Use this tool to draft feedback about Claude Code when you hit a high-signal moment. That includes both PRODUCT issues and MODEL-BEHAVIOR issues:
- a reproducible tool or product failure was just resolved or abandoned
- the user clearly expressed frustration with Claude Code or with how you handled the task
- you hit a missing capability that blocked a reasonable request
- you notice, or the user points out, that your own behavior in this session went wrong, for example: you gave a confident answer then had to retract it; you stopped short and handed work back when you could have finished; you declined or disputed a reasonable request; you spawned more subagents than the task warranted; your tone was off; you asked more clarifying questions than needed; you expanded scope beyond what was asked

The draft is QUEUED LOCALLY. It is never sent without the user's explicit approval, and calling this tool renders no UI and does not interrupt the conversation, so never announce it or ask the user about it mid-task.

Write `details` as short labeled bullets in this exact order, one to three lines each, no narrative paragraphs:
- **What happened:** the observed behavior vs. what was expected, with exact error text if short. Facts only.
- **What the user said:** the user's own words that prompted this, quoted. If nothing did, write "User didn't comment; observed by the model." Never paraphrase sentiment into a stronger claim.
- **Repro:** the minimal steps or shape that reproduces it.
- **Evidence:** identifiers a reader can chase, such as request IDs, timestamps, file paths, versions. Omit the bullet if there are none.

Constraints:
- Never fabricate or exaggerate user sentiment; report only what actually happened.
- Everything in the draft must be sourced from the user or the session, never inferred: leave unknown fields blank rather than guess, and add a final **Cause:** bullet only for a root cause you verified in-session.
- Use `area` to name the part of Claude Code the feedback is about (a feature, command, or workflow, e.g. "hooks config", "/help", "file editing") when there is a clear one; leave it blank otherwise.
- Use `failure_mode` ONLY when the report is about model behavior (how Claude responded), not a product bug. Pick the single closest value, or `other` when it is a model-behavior issue that fits no listed value; omit the field only when the report is a product/tool bug with no model-behavior component.
- Use `task_category` to name what kind of task the session was doing, or `other` when it is a clear task that fits no listed value. Omit only if genuinely unclear.
- Do not include secrets or credentials. Refer to people by role ("a teammate", "the PR reviewer"), never by name, email address, or chat/user ID. This applies inside quoted user words too: replace a name or handle with a bracketed role (e.g. "[a teammate]") and keep the rest verbatim. Do not include customer-facing channel or DM IDs, or excerpts of customer content. Session, request, and run IDs, timestamps, repo/PR numbers, and file paths (written relative to the working directory, or ~-prefixed, not absolute paths under the user's home) remain the right evidence.
- If the issue looks like a security vulnerability: describe the class of problem, never a working exploit or step-by-step extraction path.
- Draft only at the natural moments listed above, and at most one draft per distinct issue; never re-draft the same issue in a session.

## L1 in detail (for the question to Gilad)
**How many validation patients each version draws, per study group and per permutation** (n = that group's training pool):
- **Old:** `max(1, round(n × val_size / 100))`, capped at **n − 1**. A group with ≤ 1 patient gives 0.
- **New (now):** `max(1, round(n × (val_size / 100)))`, capped at **n**.

**1. The cap: only matters for tiny groups or high percentages.** At `val_size: 20`:

| n | Old (n − 1) | New (n) | Training left (old / new) |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 0 | 1 | **1 / 0** |
| 2 | 1 | 1 | 1 / 1 |
| 40 | 8 | 8 | 32 / 32 |

**Example:** a holdout on one small site, with NOT_LC = 30 patients and LC = 1 patient (P7), `val_size: 20`, 100 permutations.
- **New (cap n):** P7 is validated on every permutation, so training has **no LC patient**. The model is fitted on one class and falls back to a constant prediction at 0.5 (since W1, with a warning). All 100 permutations give a useless model, and the run still looks completed.
- **Old (cap n − 1):** P7 stays in training, so the model is real. Validation has no LC patient, so LC-side metrics (sensitivity, AUC, a fitted threshold) can't be computed.
- **Trade-off:** neither option gives a meaningful result for a one-patient group. The old cap fails more gently (a valid model, incomplete validation). **Recommendation:** `n − 1`, and possibly a warning or a stop when a group has fewer than 2 training-pool patients.

**2. Rounding:** `n × 35 / 100` and `n × 0.35` can round differently (35% of 90: old 32, new 31). Nothing breaks, but old runs with such percentages don't reproduce, and the shared random stream shifts every later permutation. The shipped 20% and 11.1111% aren't affected.

**Question for Gilad:**
1. Go back to the `n − 1` cap, and maybe warn or stop below 2 patients per group?
2. Match the old rounding?

Either change alters draws only in these edge cases, so it goes into W6 with a before/after comparison.

message.content: regarding L1, Gilad told me that the group should have at least 5, or even 10 patients. And it's only when they test on notebook, the actual dataset contains about 100 patients. So evalualte the pros and cons of cap n and capn-1 to me

content.text:
With what Gilad told you, the two caps give **the same draws on every realistic run**. So the choice is about the edge case and the cost of changing code, not about results.

**When the cap actually matters**

The cap only changes anything when `round(n × val_size / 100)` reaches `n`, i.e. when the draw would take the whole group.

| Group size n | Draw at 20% | Draw at 11.1% | val_size needed to reach the cap |
|---|---|---|---|
| 5 | 1 | 1 (minimum) | above ~90% |
| 10 | 2 | 1 | above ~95% |
| 50 | 10 | 6 | above ~99% |
| 100 | 20 | 11 | above ~99.5% |

With groups of at least 5–10 patients and our configs (20% and 11.1111%), the draw never comes close to `n`, so the two caps never differ. The cases where they do differ (1–2 patients in a group, or a very high `val_size`) only came up in the notebook tests.

**Cap n (current code)**
- **Pros:**
  - No code change and nothing to re-verify. Every run made since the change stays reproducible.
  - Same draws as cap n − 1 on real data.
- **Cons:**
  - In the edge case, a whole group can go to validation, leaving training without that class. Since W1 that gives a warning and a constant 0.5 model rather than a silent one, but the run still finishes and looks normal.

**Cap n − 1 (old code)**
- **Pros:**
  - Always leaves at least one training patient per group, so the model is always fitted on both classes.
  - Matches the old notebook behaviour.
- **Cons:**
  - A code change, regression test and before/after check for a case that real data doesn't produce.
  - In that same edge case, validation has no patient of that class, so sensitivity, AUC and the fitted threshold can't be computed. The run fails in a different place rather than working.
  - With 1 patient it still isn't a meaningful model. It only hides the problem a little better.

**My recommendation:** keep cap n and don't restore n − 1. Neither cap makes a 1–2 patient group meaningful, and on real data they're identical. What would actually help is Gilad's rule itself: a check before drawing that **warns (or stops) when a study group's training pool has fewer than 5 patients**. That catches the edge case directly instead of making it fail differently.

**What to record for L1:**
- **Cap:** WONTFIX. Groups have at least 5–10 patients in practice, so the cap never applies (per Gilad).
- **Rounding** (`n × 35 / 100` vs `n × 0.35`): also no effect at 20% or 11.1111% (the 35%-of-90 case in today's report is the only kind that differs). I'd mark it WONTFIX too, unless Gilad wants old notebook runs to reproduce exactly.
- **Optional:** the minimum-group-size warning, as a small addition in W6 if you want it.

Tell me which way you decide. I'll then update the plan and the L1 Resolution line, add the warning to W6 if you want it, and update today's daily report.

content.content:
- Found in W1 (not a finding; Tram decided 2026-11-19 to fix it here): the tuning modules don't import on master. In `FeatureTuningInput` (`balanced_rf_tuning.py`), `positive_labels` has a default and comes before `feature_run_id`, which has none (1bfe9ba). Move the field. Proof: the 3 tuning test files collect and pass. This unblocks the W7 tuning tests (H6, M12, M13, L15).

**W2. Run provenance and tracker** (Jira SW-595, Done) `[x]` (approved by Tram 2026-11-19; note: `.claude.local/reviews/review_SW-589_W2.md`)
- G13 + G18: git commit and branch on the tracker and on every run manifest.
- G18: holdouts start at feature selection. Decided with Tram (2026-11-19): the `holdout` command (no training in the plan) runs the features stage in **extract-only** mode. It writes `features_all.pkl`, `features_all_invalid.pkl`, `feature_columns.json`, the tracker and the manifest (`extract_only: true`), and skips the blind split, whole-pool selection, selector, train/test/estimation sets and stability. The runner's required artifacts become mode-aware. `resolve_feature_run` accepts an extract-only run for holdout; training on one fails with a clear error. Feature run id gets an `_extract` tag. Proof: a parity test (identical holdout results with and without whole-pool selection), a plan test, a training guard test, and the full suite. No model-number change.
- G5: keep the reader fallback for old runs. Already FIXED on master (0df6cd8); add a regression test (new runs have no base `features/` folder, old runs still load).
- G13: already FIXED on master (0df6cd8); add a regression test (commit and branch on the manifest and tracker). Same rule as M1/H6/L9: FIXED is confirmed by a test.
- G12: `n_remaining_visits`.
- M11: GRID_CLEAN drops recorded in the removal audit.
- L13: `retain_excluded_override_rows` default. Decided 2026-11-19: default `false` stays; L13 WONTFIX (2940910).

**W3. Config contract and defaults** (Jira SW-596)
- G22: validate the per-trace keys at config load.
- G3: new defaults, at most 5 default YAMLs. Agree the values with Avichai or Gilad.
- H2 → G9: trace vs. cluster model defaults, with Eran's source recorded.
- Q1: where the shipped hyperparameters came from.

**W4. Preprocessing: GRID_CLEAN, Eran's preprocessing, blip filter** (Jira SW-597)
- G10 + H4: bring in `eran_preprocess.py` from `e1a9cbd`, call it from the stage, and make GRID_CLEAN finish a realistic run.
- M6, M7: plateau median scope; persist it for inference.
- M8: end-bound check on the cut.
- M9: search-window off-by-4.
- M10: keep AUX/INDEX rows.
- L10: `median_from_up_start_to_down_start: false`.
- L11: `first_descent` naming.
- G11 + H3: enable the blip filter with the limits and actually drop rows. Make sure the temperature override doesn't reset the rows to VALID.
- L7, L8: blip counts and repair-index checks.
- Q2: was this ever run end to end? Answered by the run-through in step 5.

**W5. Feature extraction and selection** (Jira SW-598)
- H5: keep the TSF naming convention so `patient_mrmr_consensus` works.
- M3: stability uses the configured selector and doesn't swallow errors.
- M4: pre-ranking inside the bootstrap.
- M5: patient-level relevance and redundancy.
- L14: poolsel edge cases.
- G20: imputation vs. selection fill.
- G7 check: estimation rows include the filtered rows.
- Q3.

**W6. Splits, holdouts, leakage** (Jira SW-599)
- G14 + H1: record holdout membership; unbiased estimate when `blind_test_percent` > 0.
### 4a. Review checkpoint after every workstream `[ ]`
**Rule: after I commit a workstream, I stop. I don't start the next workstream until Tram explicitly approves the current one** (e.g. "W1 approved"). Silence, or approving a different workstream, isn't approval. This also covers steps 2 and 3, which together form checkpoint **W0** (tracker columns and validation).

**At the start of each workstream:**
- Tag the starting point with a local tag: `git tag sw589-W<n>-start`.
- Mark the workstream `[~]` in this plan.

**At the end of each workstream (the checkpoint):**
1. All of the workstream's commits are in, and the workstream gate (4b) passes.
2. Tag the end with a local tag: `git tag sw589-W<n>-review`. Tags aren't pushed, so they stay local.
3. Write a review note at `.claude.local/reviews/review_SW-589_W<n>.md`:
   - **Scope:** the findings covered, and each finding's new status (FIXED / INVALID / NOT REPRODUCED / WAITING + ticket).
   - **Commits:** a table of hash, finding and one-line summary.
   - **Files changed:** grouped by area, with the riskiest changes flagged first.
   - **Test evidence:**
     - new and changed tests,
     - **a per-finding table of test cases** (number of cases as pytest collects them, test file, what each covers, and whether it failed before the change), so Tram can see exactly what proves each fix (Tram's request, 2026-11-19),
     - xfail → pass transitions,
     - full-suite counts before and after,
     - the `-m invariant` / `-m system` results,
     - the synthetic run result.
   - **Metric comparison:** for workstreams that change numbers.
   - **Decisions I made,** and anything I wasn't sure about.
   - **Follow-up Jira tickets created.**
   - **Questions for Tram.**
   - **How to review:**
     - `git log --oneline sw589-W<n>-start..sw589-W<n>-review` lists the commits.
     - `git diff --stat sw589-W<n>-start..sw589-W<n>-review` shows the size.
     - `git diff sw589-W<n>-start..sw589-W<n>-review -- <path>` shows one area.
     - `git show <hash>` shows one finding.
4. Mark the workstream `[r]` (awaiting review) in this plan, then report in chat: the review note's path, a short summary, and "waiting for your approval".
5. **Stop.** No more code changes and no pushes until the workstream is approved.

**When Tram reviews:**
- **Approved:**
  - mark it `[x]`, with the approval date, in this plan and in the review note;
  - push the branch, if Tram says to;
  - start the next workstream.
- **Changes requested:**
  - Add the feedback to the review note.
  - Fix it with new commits. Don't rewrite or force-push history that has been reviewed.
  - Re-run the gate and move the review tag: `git tag -f sw589-W<n>-review`.
  - Add a "Round 2" section to the note listing only the new commits (`git diff <old review hash>..sw589-W<n>-review`), and stop again.
- **Rejected or redo:**
  - Discuss the approach first and update this plan.
  - Rolling back to `sw589-W<n>-start` rewrites history, so it needs Tram's explicit OK.

**Pushing and PRs:**
- Nothing is pushed until the workstream is approved.
- A PR (step 7) is opened only after every workstream in it is approved, and Gilad and Avichai's review comes on top of Tram's.

**Status markers:** `[r]` means awaiting Tram's review. It's added to the legend at the top.

### 4b. Test and evaluation method `[ ]`
This builds on the repo's existing conventions: `pytest.ini` markers `unit` / `invariant` / `system` / `slow`; synthetic data only, through the `make_clinical_frame` / `clinical_pickle` fixtures in `tests/conftest.py`, never real clinical files; and `xfail(strict=True)` to record confirmed defects, as SW-568 did.

**The red → green cycle for every bug finding:**
1. **Reproduce (red).** Write the smallest test that shows the defect through the real code path. Use the conditions the finding names (config flags, sensor types, traces per patient). Put it in the right folder:
   - `tests/unit/` for one function or stage,
   - `tests/invariants/` for a rule that must hold for any input (patient-level splits, row conservation, determinism),
   - `tests/system/` for end-to-end behaviour.
2. **Record it.** Mark the test `xfail(strict=True, reason="SW-589 <ID>: <defect>")`. If the fix will be in a later PR, commit the test like this, so the defect is documented in the suite and the findings file links to the test.
3. **Fix (green).** Change the code and remove the `xfail` marker. A strict xfail that suddenly passes fails the suite, so the marker can't be forgotten.
4. **Check the fix is complete and doesn't break anything else:**
   - edge cases the finding implies (NaN, empty groups, one row per class, more than one trace per patient);

### G22

**Status:** ACCEPTED · **Verified:** yes

**Resolution:** W0: partly. `validate.py:598-600` rejects `unit: trace` with `allow_multi_trace: false`; `model_reports.levels` (`:823`) is not checked against `features.unit` → W3.

**Where:** `src/core/stages/features.py:333-335 (features.unit), src/core/stages/training.py:250-261 (training.allow_multi_trace), src/core/stages/model_reports.py:141-147, 254-259, 276-280, 593-598 (model_reports.levels), src/core/stages/holdout.py:448-453, 1136-1143, src/core/train.py:2051-2056, configs/pipeline/validation_only.yaml:149, 329, 379, configs/pipeline/experiments/relive_beta_preprocess.yaml:87, 141, 166`

Per-trace is three keys that are set by hand and only checked in one direction. `features.unit: trace` extracts one row per device channel from `processed.pkl`; `cluster` extracts one row per `file_write_time` × `sensor_type` from `clustered.pkl`. `training.allow_multi_trace` null becomes true when `features.unit` is trace or when clustering is disabled (`training.py:252-255`). Explicit false with `features.unit: trace` raises (`test_trace_unit_resolves_multi_trace_and_rejects_false`). The other mismatches pass. `features.unit: cluster` with `allow_multi_trace: true` is accepted (`test_explicit_multi_trace_setting_overrides_clustering_mode`): training then requires `device_channel` and writes `trace_level_statistics` from cluster rows. Null with clustering disabled turns multi-trace on even when `features.unit` is still cluster. Holdout drops duplicate `file_write_time` rows when the flag is false (`holdout.py:448-453`), so a trace frame trained that way would keep one channel and throw the rest away; the raise above is the only thing that stops it, and it does not run if the flag is set true on a cluster frame.

`model_reports.levels` does not read either key. `trace` fails later, when `trace_level_statistics_*.csv` is missing. That file is written only when `allow_multi_trace` is true (`train.py:2051-2056`, `holdout.py:1136-1143`). The missing-file hint says the run needs `features.unit: trace`, which is the wrong gate: the flag alone writes the file, and `unit: trace` with `source: training` still cannot report traces (`run_model_reports` rejects `cluster` and `trace` unless the source is holdout; a holdout source rejects `patient`). `validation_only.yaml` ships `unit: cluster`, `allow_multi_trace` null, `levels: [patient]`. Any run that enables holdout resolves `source: auto` to holdout and then rejects `patient`. `cluster` on a trace run is valid: channels are voted to one row per `file_write_time` × `sensor_type`. `trace` on a cluster run is not.

`relive_beta_preprocess.yaml` and `relive_eran_abmerge_rest75_type2_ee.yaml` set the three keys so they agree (`unit: trace`, `allow_multi_trace: true`, `levels: [trace, cluster]`, `source: holdout`). Nothing checks that a later edit keeps them agreed. Resolve the mode from `features.unit` at config load and reject the other two keys when they disagree, before a run starts. `trace` requires `allow_multi_trace` true or null, and `levels` may be `trace` and `cluster` only, with source holdout. `cluster` requires `allow_multi_trace` false or null, and null must stay false when clustering is off; `levels` must not include `trace`.

def _resolve_config(
    merged: dict[str, Any],
    *,
    defaults_path: Path,
    run_config_path: Path | None,
    cli_overrides: Mapping[str, Any] | None,
    env: Mapping[str, str],
    now: datetime,
) -> ResolvedPipelineConfig:
    # Model YAMLs are loaded when training starts, not during feature runs.
    config = apply_dot_overrides(merged, cli_overrides)
    identity = config.setdefault("identity", {})
    dataset = config.setdefault("dataset", {})

    study = config.setdefault("study", DEFAULT_STUDY)
    gcs = config.setdefault("storage", {}).setdefault("gcs", {})
    if study in SUPPORTED_STUDIES:
        if not gcs.get("datasets_prefix"):
            gcs["datasets_prefix"] = study_datasets_prefix(study)
        if not gcs.get("results_prefix"):
            gcs["results_prefix"] = study_results_prefix(study)

    identity["owner"] = resolve_run_owner(identity.get("owner"), env=env)
    dataset["selection_id"] = _selection_id(dataset.get("include_sites"))
    # Resolve lucia / relive / lab_no_target labels before run-id tagging and
    # validation so filters and reports see concrete study_group strings.
    try:
        apply_study_profile_to_config(config)
    except ValueError as exc:
        from src.core.config.validate import ConfigValidationError

        raise ConfigValidationError(str(exc)) from exc
    if not identity.get("run_id"):
        identity["run_id"] = _generated_run_id(config, now)

    validate_pipeline_config(config)
    resolved_paths = resolve_storage_paths(config, env=env)

    dataset["gcs_uri"] = resolved_paths.dataset_gcs_uri
    dataset["local_cache_dir"] = str(resolved_paths.dataset_cache_dir)
    config["storage"]["resolved"] = resolved_paths.as_config_dict()
    config["paths"] = {
        "run_dir": str(resolved_paths.run_dir),
        "resolved_config": str(
            resolved_paths.artifacts["resolved_config"]
        ),
        "artifacts": {
            name: str(path) for name, path in resolved_paths.artifacts.items()

    options: RunnerOptions,
    config: ResolvedPipelineConfig,
) -> list[str]:
    """Resolve enabled stages in dependency order."""
    _validate_stage(options.from_stage, "from_stage")
    _validate_stage(options.to_stage, "to_stage")

    return [

    ]

docs/pipeline_review_findings.md:283:Per-trace is three keys that are set by hand and only checked in one direction. `features.unit: trace` extracts one row per device channel from `processed.pkl`; `cluster` extracts one row per `file_write_time` × `sensor_type` from `clustered.pkl`. `training.allow_multi_trace` null becomes true when `features.unit` is trace or when clustering is disabled (`training.py:252-255`). Explicit false with `features.unit: trace` raises (`test_trace_unit_resolves_multi_trace_and_rejects_false`). The other mismatches pass. `features.unit: cluster` with `allow_multi_trace: true` is accepted (`test_explicit_multi_trace_setting_overrides_clustering_mode`): training then requires `device_channel` and writes `trace_level_statistics` from cluster rows. Null with clustering disabled turns multi-trace on even when `features.unit` is still cluster. Holdout drops duplicate `file_write_time` rows when the flag is false (`holdout.py:448-453`), so a trace frame trained that way would keep one channel and throw the rest away; the raise above is the only thing that stops it, and it does not run if the flag is set true on a cluster frame.
docs/pipeline_review_findings.md:285:`model_reports.levels` does not read either key. `trace` fails later, when `trace_level_statistics_*.csv` is missing. That file is written only when `allow_multi_trace` is true (`train.py:2051-2056`, `holdout.py:1136-1143`). The missing-file hint says the run needs `features.unit: trace`, which is the wrong gate: the flag alone writes the file, and `unit: trace` with `source: training` still cannot report traces (`run_model_reports` rejects `cluster` and `trace` unless the source is holdout; a holdout source rejects `patient`). `validation_only.yaml` ships `unit: cluster`, `allow_multi_trace` null, `levels: [patient]`. Any run that enables holdout resolves `source: auto` to holdout and then rejects `patient`. `cluster` on a trace run is valid: channels are voted to one row per `file_write_time` × `sensor_type`. `trace` on a cluster run is not.
docs/pipeline_review_findings.md:287:`relive_beta_preprocess.yaml` and `relive_eran_abmerge_rest75_type2_ee.yaml` set the three keys so they agree (`unit: trace`, `allow_multi_trace: true`, `levels: [trace, cluster]`, `source: holdout`). Nothing checks that a later edit keeps them agreed. Resolve the mode from `features.unit` at config load and reject the other two keys when they disagree, before a run starts. `trace` requires `allow_multi_trace` true or null, and `levels` may be `trace` and `cluster` only, with source holdout. `cluster` requires `allow_multi_trace` false or null, and null must stay false when clustering is off; `levels` must not include `trace`.

message.content: elaborate on G22. What is the issue and what did you fix?

content.text:
**G22 in one line:** whether a run works on single traces or on clusters is described by four separate settings. Nothing checked that they agreed, so a run with contradicting settings could start and give wrong or failed results much later.

## Background: two kinds of rows

Each measurement (`file_write_time`) has several sensor channels.

- **Cluster run** (`features.unit: cluster`, clustering on): the channels are combined into one row per measurement and sensor type.
- **Per-trace run** (`features.unit: trace`): one row per channel, so several rows per measurement.

Four settings have to match this choice:

| Setting | What it controls |
|---|---|
| `features.unit` | what the features stage extracts (cluster or trace rows) |
| `pipeline.stages.clustering.enabled` | if off, channels are never combined, so rows are per channel even with `unit: cluster` |
| `training.allow_multi_trace` | whether training and holdout expect several rows per measurement |
| `model_reports.levels` / `source` | which reports to build (patient, cluster or trace) and from which stage's results |

## The issue

The only check was one rule: `unit: trace` with `allow_multi_trace: false` was rejected. Every other mismatch went through.

1. **`unit: cluster` with `allow_multi_trace: true` was accepted.** Training then treated each cluster row as a trace and wrote "trace-level statistics" that were really cluster statistics. An existing test even asserted this was allowed.
2. **Clustering off with `allow_multi_trace: false` was accepted.** Rows are per channel here, but with the flag false, holdout keeps only the first row per measurement.
   - Example: 4 channels per measurement. Holdout silently drops 3 of every 4 rows and trains on a quarter of the data. The run looks normal.
3. **The holdout-estimation tool read `null` as false**, even on per-trace runs, so its cohort had the same problem as point 2. Training resolved `null` correctly. The two paths disagreed.
4. **Report levels weren't checked at all when the config loaded.** Problems showed up only when the last stage ran, after the hours spent on training:
   - `levels: [trace]` on a cluster run failed on a missing file.
   - `patient` with a holdout source failed.
   - `cluster` with a training source failed.
   - The error message for the missing trace file pointed to the wrong setting.

## What I fixed (66e81aa)

**1. One rule, in one place.** A new function, `resolve_allow_multi_trace` in `src/core/config/validate.py`, decides the value:

| Rows are… | When | `allow_multi_trace` |
|---|---|---|
| per trace | `unit: trace`, **or** clustering off | `null` → true; true OK; **false rejected** |
| clusters | `unit: cluster` and clustering on | `null` → false; false OK; **true rejected** |

Config loading, training and the holdout-estimation tool all call this one function, so they can't disagree any more. That fixes points 1–3.

**2. Report levels are checked when the config loads.** These are now rejected before the run starts:
- `patient` together with `cluster` or `trace`: they come from different stages, so no run can build both.
- `cluster` or `trace` with `source: training`.
- `patient` with `source: holdout`.
- `trace` on a cluster run.

`source: auto` keeps its existing check at run time, because the `holdout` command decides the source only when it runs.

**3. The error message for a missing trace file** now names the real requirement: a per-trace run with `allow_multi_trace` true or null.

## Where I deviated from the finding

The finding's proposed fix says that with clustering off, `null` should resolve to false. I didn't do that. With clustering off the rows are per channel, so false causes the channel-dropping problem in point 2, which the finding itself describes. With clustering off, `null` resolves to true. Please confirm you agree. If not, it's a one-line change.

## Proof

- **New tests:** 30 cases in `tests/unit/test_trace_mode_config.py`:
  - every combination of unit, clustering and flag;
  - every report-level rule;
  - the holdout-estimation `null` case;
  - the new error message;
  - all 11 shipped configs still load.
- **Red before the fix:** 9 of the cases fail on the old code (the rejections that didn't exist, the estimation bug, the message). The others pin behaviour that has to stay the same.
- **Two old tests changed:**
  - the one asserting `cluster` with `true` is accepted now expects rejection;
  - a planning test that asked for trace reports on a cluster run now asks for cluster reports.
- **Shipped configs and results:** no shipped config is affected, and no model numbers change.

message.content: what do you mean by every other mismatch went through?

content.text:
I mean that the config loaded and the run started, with no error or warning, even when the settings contradicted each other. Only one contradiction was ever caught.

Here are all the combinations of the row type and `allow_multi_trace`, and what the old code did:

| Rows are… | `allow_multi_trace` | Agrees? | Old code |
|---|---|---|---|
| per trace (`unit: trace`) | false | No | **Rejected** (the only check) |
| clusters (`unit: cluster`, clustering on) | true | No | Accepted, ran |
| per channel (`unit: cluster`, clustering off) | false | No | Accepted, ran |

These are the mismatches between the report settings, and what happened to each:

| Report settings | Agrees? | Old code |
|---|---|---|
| `levels: [trace]` on a cluster run | No | Accepted. Failed only at the last stage (missing file) |
| `levels: [patient, cluster]` | No (needs two different sources) | Accepted. Failed at the last stage |
| `source: training` with `levels: [cluster]` | No | Accepted. Failed at the last stage |
| `source: holdout` with `levels: [patient]` | No | Accepted. Failed at the last stage |

So "went through" covers two outcomes:
- **Silently wrong results** (rows 2 and 3 of the first table). The run finishes normally: cluster rows get treated as traces, or 3 of every 4 channels are dropped. Nothing tells you.
- **A late failure** (the report rows). The error appears only after preprocessing, features and training or holdout have already run, which can be hours.

After the fix, all seven contradictions above are rejected when the config loads, before any stage runs. The one exception is the `source: auto` cases, which are still checked when the report stage runs, because the source isn't known until then.

content.text:
No. They sound like they agree, but they mean opposite things. And clustering on with `allow_multi_trace: true` is still accepted, as long as `features.unit` is `trace`.

**What the two settings mean**
- **Clustering on:** the clustering stage combines each measurement's channels into **one row** per measurement and sensor type.
- **`allow_multi_trace: true`:** tells training and holdout to expect **several rows per measurement**, one per channel. It doesn't mean "allow some extra feature"; it describes the shape of the rows.

**Which rows reach training depends on `features.unit`, not only on clustering:**

| `features.unit` | Clustering | Features read… | Rows per measurement | `allow_multi_trace: true` |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `trace` | on | `processed.pkl` (channels, before clustering) | several | **Accepted** (this is `relive_beta_preprocess.yaml`) |
| `cluster` | on | `clustered.pkl` (combined) | **one** | **Rejected** |
| `cluster` | off | `clustered.pkl` (channels passed through) | several | Accepted |

So the only rejected case is row 2: `unit: cluster` **and** clustering on **and** `true`. There the rows are combined clusters, but the flag says they're traces.

**What went wrong in that case before the fix:**
- Training requires a `device_channel` column on every row, but a cluster row stands for several channels.
- Training writes `trace_level_statistics` from those rows, so a file named "trace-level" actually holds cluster statistics, and the trace report built from it is mislabelled.

The error message for that case now says so: "features.unit=cluster with clustering enabled gives one row per cluster, so training.allow_multi_trace must be false or null (use features.unit: trace to train on single traces)".

My earlier table only said "clusters (`unit: cluster`, clustering on)", which made it look as if clustering alone decided. I should have shown the unit column too.

### G22

**Status:** FIXED · **Verified:** yes

**Resolution:** W0: partly. `validate.py:598-600` rejects `unit: trace` with `allow_multi_trace: false`; `model_reports.levels` (`:823`) is not checked against `features.unit` → W3. W3: one resolver, `resolve_allow_multi_trace` (`src/core/config/validate.py`), now used at config load, by training and by `holdout_estimation` (which read null as false). Rows are per trace when `features.unit: trace` or clustering is disabled (clustering off passes one SENSOR row per channel, so null stays true there, unlike the proposal below: false would make holdout keep one channel per `file_write_time`). - **Test:** `tests/unit/test_trace_mode_config.py` (30 cases; 9 fail before, pass after; all shipped configs still load). No model numbers change."""
s = s[:a] + new + s[b:]
d.write_text(s, encoding="utf8", newline="")
EOF

### M11
**Status:** FIXED · **Verified:** sub-review
**Resolution:** W0: open; GRID_CLEAN drops were not passed to the tracker. W2: `preprocess_dataframe_grid_clean` / `run_grid_clean_plateau_normalization` take a `tracker`, and the preprocessing stage passes its own. Each drop step records an event and the dropped traces under stage `grid_clean`, with reasons `grid_clean_median_gate`, `grid_clean_length_filter` and `grid_clean_incomplete_feature_window`. Traces are matched on `file_write_time` + `device_channel`, because the steps renumber rows. The printed messages stay. Test: `tests/unit/test_grid_clean_drop_audit.py` (3 cases; the 2 that check recording fail before, pass after). The end-to-end check, a stage run with `grid_clean` enabled, comes with the GRID_CLEAN fixes (G10/H4).
**Where:** `GRID_CLEAN drops (:413, plateau_normalization.py:425, :535-541)`
Rows dropped by median gate / length filter / incomplete windows are only printed, not recorded in the removal audit tracker.

### L2
**Status:** FIXED
**Resolution:** W0: `partition_testing.py` unchanged since the review. W1: `RotatingDrawer` now records `effective_fraction` (1 / slices) and warns when it differs from the requested proportion (30% → 3 slices of 33.3%). The method description says how slices are sized. Draws are unchanged; no shipped config uses `rotating`. Test: `tests/unit/test_partition_sizes.py` (the rotating tests fail before, pass after).
**Where:** `partition_testing.py:331`
rotating uses round(1/val_fraction) slices — 30% gives 3 slices (33%), not 30%.

### L3
**Status:** FIXED
**Resolution:** W0: still seeded only Python `random` (`stages/training.py:234-236`). W1: `_temporary_random_seed` now also seeds NumPy's global RNG and restores both states afterwards. All shipped model YAMLs set `random_state: 42` and the training path doesn't use `np.random`, so current results don't change. Test: `tests/unit/test_training_seed.py` (fails before, passes after).
**Where:** `stages/training.py:218-224`
_temporary_random_seed seeds only Python random, not NumPy; fine today (drawers use random, models have random_state), fragile if any code uses np.random.

### L4
**Status:** FIXED
**Resolution:** W1: the aggregate keeps its fields, so existing callers (`notebooks/pipeline/full/04_training.ipynb`, the model-report stage) don't break. It now names the model they describe (`aggregate_model_id`), adds `results_by_model()`, and warns when more than one model was trained. Test: `tests/unit/test_training_stage.py::test_multi_model_aggregate_says_which_model_it_describes` and `::test_single_model_aggregate_does_not_warn` (fail before, pass after). Found while fixing: with `source: training` and several models, `model_reports` builds its report from `output_dir` alone, i.e. for the last model only → W8.
**Where:** `stages/training.py:781, 806`
Aggregate TrainingResult.results/artifacts = last model only; callers using it with multiple selected_models silently see one model.

### L5
**Status:** FIXED
**Resolution:** W0: partly. `threshold_fallback_` was recorded (`train.py:155-156`) but no warning was raised. W1: `ThresholdClassifier.fit` now raises a `UserWarning` naming the unmet constraints, and sets `threshold_fallback_reason_ = "constraints_unmet"`. The reason is also written to the per-model table next to `threshold_fallback`. Test: `tests/unit/test_threshold_fallback.py` (fails before, passes after).
**Where:** `train.py:122-127`
If no threshold meets min_sens/min_spec, threshold silently stays 0.5.

### L6
**Status:** FIXED
**Resolution:** W0: open. The early returns (`train.py:99-114`) set 0.5 without setting `threshold_fallback_`. W1: both early returns now set `threshold_fallback_ = True` and a reason (`single_class` or `too_few_patients`), and raise a `UserWarning` that says why. Same shared helper as L5. Test: `tests/unit/test_threshold_fallback.py` (fails before, passes after).
**Where:** `train.py:91-95`
New fallback: if a class has `<2` rows, skip calibration and use 0.5 silently.

### L9
**Status:** FIXED
**Resolution:** W0: code reading shows the fix in aac57b7. `_finite_index` / `_finite_tuple` return None for missing landmarks (`trigger_detection.py:139-157`). W1: regression test `tests/unit/test_trigger_detection_anchors.py::test_missing_landmark_does_not_abort_the_cohort` (NaN up/down trigger, missing up/down tuple). It fails on aac57b7^ with `ValueError: cannot convert float NaN to integer` and passes on master.
**Where:** `trigger_detection.py:150`
NaN up_trig/down_trig crashes the whole detection (int(NaN)).

### L12
**Status:** FIXED
**Resolution:** W0: partly. `src/core/pipeline.py` was removed (1bfe9ba). `sensor_fusion.py:32` still defaulted to `mode="late"`, which raises (`:59`); nothing imports the module. W1: `apply_sensor_fusion` now defaults to `mode="none"`, the only implemented mode. Removed modes still raise when asked for explicitly. Test: `tests/unit/test_sensor_fusion.py` (failed before the change, passes after).
**Where:** `sensor_fusion.py:58-61`
late/early/autoencoder/leak_free fusion now raise NotImplementedError but mode="late" is still the default in sensor_fusion.py:32/pipeline.py:259.

### L16
**Status:** FIXED
**Resolution:** W1: documented rather than rewired. `verify_partitions` has two callers. `test_partitions` passes it the partitions it just drew, so it can only test the draw scheme (the finding). `partition_report` passes a completed run's recorded splits, which is a real audit. The result now has `scope` (`planned` / `recorded_run`) and a `scope_note`, and the HTML report shows the note under the PASS/FAIL banner. For `planned`, the note names the guards that actually check a run: `validate_feature_split_leaks` (`v2_pipeline_run.py:1293`) and the train/test overlap check (`train.py:1780`). Test: `tests/unit/test_partition_audit_scope.py` (fails before, passes after).
**Where:** `partition_testing.verify_partitions`
verify_partitions is true by construction; audits its own carved test set and RNG stream, not the trained splits. Real guards are in v2_pipeline_run.py:1216-1232 and train.py:2017.

### L19
**Status:** FIXED
**Resolution:** W0: still pointed at `configs/experiments/pipeline_lucia_grid_clean_preprocess.yaml` (`GRID_CLEAN_PREPROCESSING.md:78`), which does not exist. W1: the Scope and Configuration sections now use the Pipeline V2 keys (`preprocessing.grid_clean.*`, `preprocessing.blip_filter.*`, `preprocessing.channel_type_filter`). They point at `validation_only.yaml` for the defaults and at the two experiment YAMLs that enable GRID_CLEAN. Test: `tests/unit/test_grid_clean_doc.py` checks that every path, function and `preprocessing.*` key the doc names exists, and that no `process.` / `filter.` / `load.` keys remain (fails before, passes after).
**Where:** `docs`
GRID_CLEAN_PREPROCESSING.md references a non-existent config file and LuciaPipeline-style keys.
## Confirmed correct (no action)
- Default preprocessing path (grid_clean/blip off) matches pipeline_v2_preprocessing.ipynb step-by-step.
- Clustering stage matches pipeline_v2_clustering.ipynb (cohesive + weighted_mean, unchanged algorithm).
- plateau_normalization.py is a faithful move; eran_ali→crop_pad rename is backward compatible (anything ≠ cubic = crop/pad).
- data_splitting.py is identical to the old blind_split.choose_test_files / train_test_split_by_file (unused helpers dropped, nothing imports them).
- RandomDrawer reproduces the old per-permutation validation sampling for default val_size=20, same global RNG.
- Labels 1/2 → 0/1 encoding correct throughout training, tuning (XGBoost safe), poolsel OOB AUC, and ROC (pos_label).
- PPV/NPV Bayes formulas, top_left/youden/manual thresholds correct; default roc_curve_set: validation → test metrics not threshold-leaked.
- Patient-level aggregation keeps train/validation/test separate.
- Tuning folds are truly StratifiedGroupKFold by patient; blind test never touched during tuning.
- XGBoost CPU accelerator mapping doesn't change predictions (xgboost 3.0.2).
- No remaining code imports any of the ~130 deleted Python modules.
## Questions for the author
1. Where do the shipped BRF/XGB hyperparameters and n_features: 20 / L-RAD / permutations: 200 come from (tuning run id, feature run, score)? Should defaults revert to the notebook values? **SW-589:** → W3

Review `impute_with_selector` and its effect on feature selection. It does not change which features are chosen. `select_features` (holdout: `_select_holdout_features`) finishes first; `fit_selector(..., feature_names=selected)` only stores medians; `impute_with_selector` then `fillna`s the train, test, and estimation frames. The effect is that selection scores one fill and the model trains on another. Ensemble and the other rankers run `_clean_features` on a copy: median when a column is under 10% missing, 0 otherwise. `patient_mrmr_consensus` skips that call, but poolsel's `clean_matrix` fills every NaN with 0 before scoring, and `clean_feature_frame` uses the same 10% rule before the redundancy step. That copy is thrown away. The medians written onto `FeatureSelectorState` are the raw training-column medians (NaNs skipped), and `impute_with_selector` applies that median to every selected column, including columns selection filled with 0. A feature can win the funnel on zero-filled values and then be fit on median-filled values. The medians are taken on the whole train+validation pool, so the later validation split is filled with constants that validation rows helped set. The blind test and the estimation set do not contribute, which is correct. A selected column that is entirely NaN stores `nan`, and `fillna` leaves it missing, so Easy Ensemble still sees the NaN it was meant to remove. Make the matrix that is scored and the matrix that is trained the same fill, or record the difference as intentional.

Holdout drops duplicate `file_write_time` rows when the flag is false (`holdout.py:448-453`), so a trace frame trained that way would keep one channel and throw the rest away; the raise above is the only thing that stops it, and it does not run if the flag is set true on a cluster frame.

content.text:
The code makes no distinction today. Every run, per-trace or per-cluster, trains whatever `training.selected_models` lists. The model file names suggest which run type each set was made for, but nothing enforces it.

**What the names suggest** (from the comments in `validation_only.yaml`):

| Model files | Meant for | In the default list? |
|---|---|---|
| `balanced_rf_aggregated_tuned_lucia_legacy`, `xgboost_aggregated_tuned_lucia_legacy`, `easy_ensemble_tuned_lucia_legacy` | **per-cluster**: "aggregated" = trained on the combined cluster signal (the notebook models) | **Yes** (all 3) |
| `balanced_rf_trace_based_legacy`, `xgboost_trace_based_legacy` | **per-trace**: "the trace-based tuned values" | No (commented out) |
| `random_forest_adapted`, `easy_ensemble_adapted`, `xgboost_adapted` | the FO1 `adapted_final_all_breath` profile (TYPE1-61). The names don't say which run type | No |

**What the shipped configs actually use:**

| Config | Run type | Models it trains |
|---|---|---|
| `validation_only.yaml` (defaults), `example_run_lucia.yaml`, `example_run_relive.yaml`, the 5 `lucia550` holdout experiments | per-cluster | the 3 `*aggregated*` / `easy_ensemble_tuned` (matches) |
| `relive_beta_preprocess.yaml` | **per-trace** | the 3 `*_adapted`, not the trace-based ones |
| `type1_61_crop_wp_m1_a070_pw2.yaml` | per-cluster | the 3 `*_adapted` |
| `example_lab_no_target.yaml` | **per-cluster** | the 2 **`*_trace_based_legacy`** (trace models on a cluster run) |

Two things don't match the naming:
- The only per-trace experiment (`relive_beta_preprocess.yaml`) doesn't use the trace-based models.
- `example_lab_no_target.yaml` uses the trace-based models on a cluster run.

That may be deliberate, for example if the `*_adapted` profile turned out better on traces, but nothing in the repo says so.

**What this means for G9:** the finding asks for two default sets, picked automatically. The obvious split would be:
- **per-cluster:** the 3 `*aggregated*` / `easy_ensemble_tuned` (today's default);
- **per-trace:** the 2 `*_trace_based_legacy`.

Only Eran can confirm that split, including whether the per-trace set should be the trace-based models or `*_adapted`, and say where the trace-based values came from. I'd add that to question 3 for Eran: **"Which models should be the per-trace default: `*_trace_based_legacy` or `*_adapted`, and what run and metric are the values from?"**

# The depth-2 booster of the ERAN57 breath-point W4 wave, as the campaign's

# Shallower and slower than xgboost_adapted (depth 2 against 3, 300 rounds at

# published operating point is read later, from the probabilities, at the

I checked every branch in the repo, local and remote. **No: Eran has never added trace-based models.** The two trace-based model files are Gilad's, and every model file Eran did add is used only in cluster runs.

**Who added the trace-based model files**

| File | Added by | Commit |
|---|---|---|
| `balanced_rf_trace_based_legacy.yaml` | **Gilad** | 0df6cd8 (2026-10-29), "Keep the full cohort through preprocessing and record git identity on each run" |
| `xgboost_trace_based_legacy.yaml` | **Gilad** | same commit |

Their values (BRF 450 trees / depth 3, XGB 150 / depth 2) are the earlier "tuned" defaults that H2 describes. In 0df6cd8 they were renamed to `*_trace_based_legacy` when the notebook models became the default. Neither file records where the values came from.

**Every model file Eran has added (all branches)**

| File | Commit | On master? | Run type it's used in |
|---|---|---|---|
| `random_forest_adapted.yaml`, `xgboost_adapted.yaml` | 95e3e71 (2026-11-01), TYPE1-61 | Yes | `type1_61_crop_wp_m1_a070_pw2.yaml`: **cluster** (no `unit` set, clustering on) |
| `xgboost_depth2_mds.yaml` | d484e29 (2026-11-18), ERAN57 | **No**: only on `eran/breath-point-default-on-master` and `eran/eran-reports-companion` | `eran57_bp_w4_nosm_a050_bp.yaml`: **cluster** (no `unit` set) |
| `random_forest_NFLD/lung`, `xgboost_NFLD/lung` | c799770 (2026-01-21) | old `configs/models/` layout, before Pipeline V2 | older pipeline |

`easy_ensemble_adapted.yaml` was added by Gilad in 1bc55dd ("Name Eran's adapted models by their model id"). It's based on Eran's adapted profile.

**The one per-trace experiment** (`relive_beta_preprocess.yaml`) is Gilad's (c0cf8ac, 7730944). It uses Eran's `*_adapted` models, which Eran tuned on cluster runs.

**What this means for G9:** the finding's note "waits for Eran's trace-based models to be added" is still true. No per-trace model set from Eran exists anywhere in the repo. What exists:
- Gilad's two `*_trace_based_legacy` files, with no recorded source;
- Eran's `*_adapted` models, tuned for cluster runs and reused on one per-trace experiment.

So G9 is genuinely blocked on Eran. I'd mark it **WAITING (Eran)**. The questions for him become:
1. Will you provide per-trace models, or are the `*_adapted` ones meant for per-trace runs too?
2. Should the two `*_trace_based_legacy` files stay? Neither of you added their values with a source.

Layout `data-type` values are `layout-two-equal`, `layout-two-left-sidebar`,
`layout-two-right-sidebar`, `layout-three-equal`, `layout-three-with-sidebars`, and
`layout-section`; supply the matching number of column children. Columns accept
percentage `data-width`; preserve non-standard widths emitted with `layout-section`.
Sections accept `data-column-rule-style="solid"`.

Task lists and items accept `data-local-id`; omitted schema-required IDs are generated.

### Numeric attributes

Write scalar sizing attributes as unitless finite decimals (`data-width="80.5"`,
not `"80px"` or `"80%"`). Invalid values are dropped; fractions are preserved.

### Breakout (wide / full-width elements)

Use `data-breakout="wide"` or `"full-width"`; optional `data-breakout-width` is pixels: positive by default, finite with round-trip fixes.

Root `
` (not nested expand), `
`, `
`, panel `
` and `
` support breakout. Other nesting ignores it.

### Block marks

Paragraphs support these style-based marks; headings support alignment or indentation.
Alignment and indentation cannot be combined.

Round-trip fixes preserve table/extension `data-fragment-marks='[{"localId":"ID","name":"optional"}]'`, extension `data-mark`/`data-sources`, media `data-border-size` (1-3)/`data-border-color` (hex6/8), and block-media `data-annotations='[{"id":"ID","annotationType":"inlineComment"}]'`. Keep IDs/order and annotation/color whitespace. Root extensions also accept breakout.

## Inline elements

| Element | HTML Pattern |
|---------|-------------|
| Bold | `text` |
| Italic | `text` |
| Underline | `text` |
| Strikethrough | `text` |
| Inline code | `text` |
| Subscript | `text` |
| Superscript | `text` |
| Highlight | `text` — see **Highlight colors** below |
| Text color | `text` — see **Text colors** below |
| Link | `text` |
| Same-page heading | `text` — see note below |
| Line break | `
` |
| Status lozenge | `Done`; style is optional |
| Emoji | `🚀` |
| Date | `March 15, 2025` |
| Mention | `@Name` |
| Inline comment | `text` |
| Placeholder | `Type something…` |

**Inline code:** `` cannot carry other inline formatting except an annotation span.
Conflicting marks are dropped; for ``, the link is kept and code styling is dropped.

**Highlight:** `` converts to off-palette `#FFFF00`; emit it only to retain an
existing ``, never for new highlights.

**Links and smart cards:** A plain `` produces a standard hyperlink.
Same-page heading jumps use a hash href, not a full URL:

```html

See the appendix and more detail.


Appendix


…


More detail

```

The href is `#` plus the heading text with whitespace replaced by hyphens
(`
More detail
` → `#More-detail`). Duplicate headings on the same page
append `.1`, `.2` (`#Appendix.1`). Do **not** write `§`, "section 9", or invented
numbers — those are not links. Do **not** put spaces in the hash (`#More detail`
will not match the rendered heading id).

Add `data-card-appearance` to produce a smart-link card:

| `data-card-appearance` | ADF node | Renders as |
|---|---|---|
| `inline` | `inlineCard` | an inline pill, sized to sit inside a sentence |
| `block` | `blockCard` | a standalone summary card — title, icon, description |
| `embed` | `embedCard` | a live, playable full view |

`block` and `embed` are block-level nodes, so put the anchor on its own rather than
mid-sentence; the converter splits a paragraph around one. All three appearances render from the URL, so anchor text is dropped —
write `` and leave it empty.
Use HTTP(S) or scheme-relative URLs for cards; other schemes are dropped from
embed cards and card link shorthands. Embed cards accept `data-layout`
(`center` by default, `wide`, `full-width`, `wrap-left`, `wrap-right`, `align-start`,
`align-end`), `data-width` (0–100), and numeric `data-original-width` /
`data-original-height`; the same attributes work on the canonical embed `
`.

**Emoji:** `data-shortname` is required. Give both `data-emoji-id` (hyphen-joined hex
codepoints such as `1f680`, or an `atlassian-*` name) and `data-emoji-text` for the same
emoji, or neither so the converter fills them from the shortname. Confluence renders the
id, falling back to the text.

**Date:** always use `` for actual calendar dates; never
plain text. Do not wrap durations, versions, or non-date values.

**Status colors:** `neutral`, `purple`, `blue`, `red`, `yellow`, `green`

**Mention attributes:** `data-user-id` (required), `data-access-level` (optional),
`data-user-type` (optional). See **Output rules → Mentions** before emitting a
mention.

**Inline comments:** Annotation spans are inline-only anchors requiring
`data-annotation-id` and `data-annotation-type="inlineComment"`. They wrap text or a whole
mention, status, date, emoji, inline media, or inline card element. The same ID may occur
on several spans; preserve each when editing around it, and never create or retarget one.

green `#006644`, Bold orange `#ff991f`, Bold red `#bf2600`, Bold purple `#403294`,

**Highlight colors:** Gray `#dcdfe4`, Teal `#c6edfb`, Lime `#d3f1a7`, Yellow
`#f8e6a0`, Orange `#fedec8`, Magenta `#fdd0ec`, Purple `#dfd8fd`

Only use the respective palette above when authoring or changing inline text or
highlight colors.

## Nesting rules (ADF schema)

Each row lists the direct children to author; other nesting is rejected. Tables in
panels stay excluded for editor compatibility, though the schema accepts them in
existing content.

If a composition is unsupported, change the layout to use allowed nesting.
Do not wrap unsupported content in a migration extension.

**Core blocks** are paragraph, heading, bullet/ordered/task/decision list, code block,
media single/group, blockquote, panel, and rule.

| Container | Allowed children |
| --- | --- |
| Paragraph, task/decision item, heading | All inline nodes; `
`/`
` wrappers in a task item are flattened. |
| Caption | Formatted text/code, hard break, mention, emoji, date, placeholder, inline card, status; not inline media/extension. |
| Block task item | Paragraph children. |
| Ordinary list item `
  • ` | Paragraph, bullet/ordered/task list, code block, media single. |
| Blockquote | Paragraph, bullet/ordered list, code block, media single/group. |
| Panel | Paragraph, heading, bullet/ordered/task/decision list, code block, media single/group, block card, rule. Not table, expand, blockquote, embed card, or nested panel. |
| Expand | Core blocks, block/embed card, table, nested expand. |
| Table cell/header | Core blocks, block/embed card, nested expand. |
| Nested expand | Core blocks. |
| Layout column | Core blocks, block/embed card, table, expand. |
| Layout section | Layout column children only. |

In an ordinary list item, bare inline content becomes a paragraph; close the list
before adding a block absent from its allow-list. For task indentation, put the nested
task `
      ` after its preceding `
    • ` within the parent task list, not inside that item.

Lists, tables, task and decision lists, layout sections and columns, list items,
table cells and headers, blockquotes, panels, expands and media groups must hold at
least one child. Converters give an empty wrapper that admits a paragraph an empty
`
      `, and drop other empty containers.

## Tables

Use `` for header cells, in a header row or column; rows may be bare children of
`` or grouped in `` / ``. Optional table features:

- `data-number-column="true"`/`"false"` turns row numbers on/off; `data-display-mode="fixed"` locks
  column widths.
- Merge cells with `rowspan` / `colspan` on `
      ` / ``.
- `data-colwidth` sets per-column pixel widths on each cell, with or without fixed
  display mode; a spanning cell uses a comma-separated list such as `"120,240"`.
- **Preserve `data-colwidth` when editing a table** — copy every cell's value verbatim
  unless asked to resize columns;
  dropping it resets the table to evenly distributed columns.
- Numeric `data-width`; `data-layout`: `default`, `center`, `wide`, `full-width`,
  `align-start`, or `align-end`. Keep layout on edits.
- Cell background uses `data-background="#DEEBFF"`; vertical alignment uses
  `data-valign` (`top`, `middle`, or `bottom`).

**Supported background colors:** when authoring or changing a table cell background or
custom panel `data-color`, only use the following palette. The Editor maps these stored ADF
hex values to theme-aware design tokens when rendering.
White `#FFFFFF`, Light gray `#F4F5F7`, Gray `#B3BAC5`,
Light blue `#DEEBFF`, Blue `#B3D4FF`, Dark blue `#4C9AFF`,
Light teal `#E6FCFF`, Teal `#B3F5FF`, Dark teal `#79E2F2`,
Light green `#E3FCEF`, Green `#ABF5D1`, Dark green `#57D9A3`,
Light yellow `#FFFAE6`, Yellow `#FFF0B3`, Dark yellow `#FFC400`,
Light red `#FFEBE6`, Red `#FFBDAD`, Dark red `#FF8F73`,
Light purple `#EAE6FF`, Purple `#C0B6F2`, Dark purple `#998DD9`.

## Media / Attachment elements

Upload a page attachment first, then use its returned `MEDIA_ID` and `COLLECTION`
(`contentId-` is typical for native attachments):

| Display | HTML pattern |
| --- | --- |
| Image | `` |
| File card/group | `
      ` |
| Inline file or image | `
      See .
      ` |

Repeat the media child for multiple files; append ``
inside a figure for a caption. Figure layout is `center` (default), `wrap-left`, `wrap-right`,
`wide`, `full-width`, `align-start`, or `align-end`. Pair any figure `data-width`
with `data-width-type="percentage"` (positive width up to 100) or `"pixel"`
(positive pixel width). For new images, prefer percentage widths: `80` for
charts/diagrams, `60` for screenshots, `40`–`50` for smaller images; use `100` sparingly.

Round-trip fixes opt-in preserves empty collections.
File media `
      ` and inline `` bodies stay empty. Their optional attributes
are `data-alt` (alt text), `data-occurrence-key` (tracks multiple references to the same
media), and intrinsic pixel `data-width` / `data-height`;
figure display sizing belongs on the figure, inline dimensions on the ``.
Inline `data-media-type` is optional: `file` renders a filename chip, `image` the image
itself in text, or `link`. If omitted, Confluence resolves rendering from the file.
Preserve its value or absence when editing: adding `file` to an untyped inline image
turns it into a filename chip. Do not use a relative
`` or `/wiki/download/attachments/…` URL for attachments.

External images need no upload: ``. Bare or figure-wrapped images become
`mediaSingle > media[type=external]`.

## Output rules

**Output shape** — Emit an HTML body fragment only: do not wrap it in ``,
``, or ``, and do not wrap it in Markdown code fences.

**Local IDs (`data-local-id`)** — Targetable nodes carry a `data-local-id`. A local
ID is the **final 12-character segment of a UUID** (lowercase hexadecimal, e.g.
`a1b2c3d4e5f6`). Preserve fetched IDs. Omit them on new nodes unless another operation
must target the node; then generate one random 12-character lowercase hex value and
reuse it for that reference. The converter generates other schema-required IDs.

**Mentions** — `data-user-id` requires a real Atlassian account ID (AAID). Do **not**
invent one; if unknown, write plain text such as `[@assignee]` instead of a mention.

**Smart links** — Prefer an inline smart link to a raw hyperlink whenever possible. For a
bare URL, a link alone in a paragraph or list item, or an entry in a sources / related-links
list or table, emit a smart link, which already displays the target's readable live title,
icon, and preview. Do not duplicate the page name beside the card:

```html

        
  
        • 

      
```

Use `inline` by default, `block` for a single link the page is highlighting. Keep a plain
`text` only when the anchor text has to read as part of a sentence — a
card drops that text. When editing fetched content, leave existing plain links alone
unless asked.

**Full-view embeds** — Video, recording, and Confluence whiteboard, database, or app URLs (Loom,
YouTube, Vimeo, Drive, …) default to an embed card, so the full view renders in
place:

```html

```

This holds however the URL reached you; `inline`, a block card, and a plain
`` each render a partial card the reader must click through. When editing
fetched content, keep an existing appearance unless asked to make it viewable in
place.
